questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(1,\sqrt{3}).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the point $P$ lies in the first quadrant, we can determine $\theta $ by taking the arctangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(2,\frac{\pi }{3}).$

questions.problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(\sqrt{2}t,\sqrt{2}t),$ where $t$ is a positive real number. Find the polar coordinates of $P$ expressed in terms of $t.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

Expressed in terms of $t,$ the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}t)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the point $P$ lies in the first quadrant, we can determine $\theta $ by taking the arctangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}t}{\sqrt{2}t}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(2t,\frac{\pi }{4}).$

questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(4,-1).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$ Round your answer to two decimal places where necessary.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+1} \\  & =\sqrt{17} \\  & =4.123\,10… \\  & ≈4.12\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{4})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-0.25)| \\  & =|-0.244\,97…| \\  & ≈0.244\,97\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point lies in the fourth quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -0.244\,97 \\  & ≈6.04\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(4.12,6.04),$ rounded to two decimal places.

questions.problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(\sqrt{3}k,-k),$ where $k$ is a positive real number. Find the polar coordinates of $P$ expressed in terms of $k.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

Expressed in terms of $k,$ the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}k)^{2}+(-k)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3{k}^{2}+{k}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{k}^{2}} \\  & =2k\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-k}{\sqrt{3}k})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =|-\frac{\pi }{6}| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point lies in the fourth quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{11\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(2k,\frac{11\pi }{6}).$

questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(5,5).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2\cdot {5}^{2}} \\  & =5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the point $P$ lies in the first quadrant, we can determine $\theta $ by taking the arctangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{5}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(5\sqrt{2},\frac{\pi }{4}).$

questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-\frac{k}{4},\frac{k}{2}),$ where $k$ is a positive real number. What are the polar coordinates of $P?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer where necessary.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{k}{4})}^{2}+{(\frac{k}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{k}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{k}^{2}}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{5\cdot \frac{{k}^{2}}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}\,k}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{(\frac{k}{2})}{(-\frac{k}{4})})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-2)| \\  & ≈1.107.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi $ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -1.107 \\  & ≈2.035 \\  & ≈2,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer. Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\sqrt{5}\,k}{4},2).$

questions.problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-\sqrt{3},-1).$ Find the polar coordinates of $P.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{-\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the third quadrant, we add the reference angle to $\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(2,\frac{7\pi }{6}).$

questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-a,a),$ where $a$ is a positive real number. What are the polar coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-a)^{2}+{a}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{a}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,a.\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{-a})| \\  & =|-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,a,\frac{3\pi }{4}).$

questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-2a,a),$ where $a$ is a positive real number. What are the polar coordinates of $P?$  Round your answer to the nearest tenth where appropriate.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2a)^{2}+{a}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{a}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\text{ }\,a.\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{-2a})| \\  & =|-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{2})| \\  & ≈0.463\,6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & ≈\pi -0.463\,6 \\  & ≈2.7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(\sqrt{5}\text{ }\,a,2.7).$

A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-1,0).$ Find the polar coordinates of $P.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies on the negative half of the $x$-axis, we have $\theta =\pi .$ 

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(1,\pi ).$

canonical_examples.problem: Express the Cartesian point $P (1,-\sqrt{3})$ in polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first thing to realize is that the point $P$ lies in the fourth quadrant.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13951963/assets/e346dd6ef21e29cc438747c13907c93b8a2b795f01bd360bed8b9319c514fa24.png)

First, we determine $r\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		r &= \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\[3pt]
		&= \sqrt{1^2 + (-\sqrt{3})^2}\[3pt]
		&=\sqrt{1+3}\[3pt]
		&= 2
	}
$$

We then compute the reference angle $\theta_R\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		\theta_R &= \left|\arctan\left(\dfrac y x\right)\right|\
		 &= \left|\arctan\left(\dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{1}\right)\right|\
		 &= \left|\arctan\left(-\sqrt 3\right)\right|\
		 &= \left|-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right|\

		&= \dfrac{\pi}{3}
	}
$$

Since the point lies in the fourth quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $\left(2, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right).$

canonical_examples.problem: Express the Cartesian point $P (-6, 8)$ in polar coordinates. Round your answer to three decimal places where appropriate.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13951963/assets/a035983487fde24bd9f813026c50948ee8601dd81e21bb7307ec03ad746ac63b.png)

First, we determine $r\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		r &= \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\[3pt]
		&= \sqrt{(-6)^2 + 8^2}\[3pt]
		&=\sqrt{100}\[3pt]
		&= 10
	}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\theta_R &= \left|\arctan\left(\dfrac y x\right)\right|\[3pt]
		&= \left|\arctan\left(-\dfrac 8{6}\right)\right|\[3pt]
		&\approx 0.927\,29 .
	}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -0.927\,29 \\  & ≈2.214\,29 \\  & ≈2.214\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places. Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(10,2.214).$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		r &= \sqrt{0^2 + (-7)^2}\
		&= \sqrt{7^2}\
		&= 7
	}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies on the negative half of the $y$-axis, we have $\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}.$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $\left(7, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right).$
